_comment: Production series, film 4: slides and a short run in FreeXmlToolkit (FundsXmlProdGeneratingDocVideo) on files written by the reference export (Example-Export_Multi-Asset_2025-10*.xml).

description.en: How to produce FundsXML from a database: start with the target file, a mapping table, which data goes to whom, templates, XSLT or generated code, ControlData, the reference export, element order, empty elements and formats, validation in FreeXmlToolkit, corrections, large deliveries, several schema versions, partner configuration, time windows, golden-file tests and CI, handing over, resends and documentation.

say.en: Now the other direction: the data is in your database, and a partner expects a FundsXML file. In this film you see the ways to generate FundsXML, the mapping behind it, how to handle several schema versions and large files, and how to test the result.

items.head: An official example file
items.text: Close to what the partner expects.

items.head: Agreed with the partner
items.text: Before the first line of code.

say.en: Start with the target, not with the code. Take an official example file that comes close to what your partner expects, for example one of the realistic samples in the FundsXML examples repository. It shows which elements a complete delivery uses, in which order. Agree it with your partner, and you know what to build before the first line of code.

Then the mapping: for each element, where does the value come from? A simple table does the job: the database column, the FundsXML path, and the rule, such as a conversion or a fixed value. This table is the most important document of the project. It is also what the business side reviews, long before any file exists.

items.head: The partner register
items.text: Funds, kinds of data, version, templates.

items.head: One delivery per partner and type
A new fund for a partner
items.text: A change in the register, not in the code.

say.en: Which data goes to whom? The partner register answers it: which funds a partner receives, which kinds of data, which version and which templates. The generator reads the register and builds one delivery per partner and type. Adding a fund for a partner is then a change in the register, not in the code.

en.title: Three ways to write the file

items.head: Templates
items.text: XML written directly from the query results.

items.head: Generated code
items.text: Classes from the schema: JAXB, xsdata.

say.en: There are three common ways to write the file. Templates write the X M L directly from the query results; simple and easy to read. X S L T transforms an intermediate X M L, for example from the database, into FundsXML. And code generators create classes from the schema, with JAXB in Java or xsdata in Python; the code then fills objects and writes them out.

items.head: Templates
items.text: Small and medium deliveries; you see the XML.

items.head: XSLT
items.text: When the data is XML already.

items.head: Generated code
items.text: Type safety, but large code, regenerated for every version.

say.en: Which one fits? Templates suit small and medium deliveries and teams that like to see the X M L. X S L T suits setups where the data is already X M L. Generated code gives type safety, but the FundsXML schema is large, so the generated code is too, and it must be regenerated for every new version.

en.title: ControlData of every file
en.code:
<ControlData>
  <UniqueDocumentID>EXAMPLE-HUB-f5c56ecd-…</UniqueDocumentID>     new for every file
  <DocumentGenerated>2026-11-26T14:16:26+00:00</DocumentGenerated>   now
  <Version>4.2.9</Version>
  <ContentDate>2025-10-31</ContentDate>                              the data's date
  <DataSupplier>...EXAMPLE-HUB...</DataSupplier>
  <DataOperation>INITIAL</DataOperation>                             AMEND for a correction
</ControlData>

say.en: Every file begins with ControlData. Generate a new document ID for every file, never reuse one. The generation time is now; the content date is the date the data is valid for, which is usually earlier. Name the data supplier. And set the data operation: initial for a first delivery, amend for a correction, with the ID of the delivery it corrects.

en.title: The reference export: a share class
en.code:
def share_class(sc, price, navs, fund_ccy, action):
    return el("ShareClass",
              el("Identifiers", el("ISIN", sc["isin"])),
              el("Names", el("OfficialName", sc["name"])),
              el("Currency", sc["currency"]),
              el("Prices", price and el("Price",
                 el("ActionCode", action),
                 el("NavDate", price["nav_date"]),
                 el("PriceCurrency", price["currency"]),
                 el("PriceNature", price["price_type"]),
                 el("NavPrice", price["value"]))),
              total_asset_value(navs, fund_ccy, sc["currency"]))

# el() leaves out elements without a value

say.en: The reference implementation uses templates. This one writes a share class with its prices: the identifiers, the currency, and the net asset value per date. The values come from the tables you saw in the earlier films. The order of the elements follows the schema exactly, because X S D sequences are strict.

The order matters more than many expect. Here two elements of a share class were written the wrong way round. The schema does not accept it: the validator reports invalid content, and names the element it expected instead. The fix is in the generator, which must follow the sequence of the schema exactly, element by element.

en.title: Leave out what you do not have

items.head: No empty elements
items.text: Empty is not the same as missing, and often invalid.

items.head: A required element without a value
items.text: Fix the data, not the file.

say.en: A rule that saves many errors: leave out what you do not have. An empty element is not the same as a missing one, and it often fails validation. Never write placeholders such as N A or zero. And if a required element has no value, the problem is in the data; fix it there, not in the file.

Formats are the next source of trouble. Numbers use a decimal point and no thousands separators, whatever the language settings of the server. Dates are written year, month, day. Booleans are true or false. The file is U T F eight. And percentages are plain numbers, without a percent sign.

Here is the generated file, opened in FreeXmlToolkit. Validation against the schema: valid. The data-quality check: no errors. Every generated file goes through exactly these checks before it leaves the house, automatically.

items.head: A new file, a new document ID
The complete corrected data
items.text: For that fund and date, not one number.

say.en: Corrections are generated too. A correction is a new file with its own document ID, the data operation amend, and the ID of the delivery it corrects. It carries the complete corrected data for that fund and date, not just the one changed number. Then the receiver can simply replace what it has, as you saw in the film about loading.

items.head: Write as a stream
items.text: XMLStreamWriter in Java, lxml xmlfile in Python.

items.head: Split very large deliveries
items.text: For example one file per fund.

say.en: For large deliveries, write the file as a stream too: with the X M L stream writer in Java, or incremental writing in Python. Generate one fund at a time, so that memory stays small. Very large deliveries can be split, for example one file per fund. And compress the file for transport.

items.head: One generator
items.text: Differences in a table, not a copy.

say.en: Partners expect different versions. Keep one generator and describe the differences between the versions in a table, rather than copying the whole generator. New elements in FundsXML are usually optional, so a newer version mostly adds fields. Test every version you deliver, against its own schema.

items.head: No copy of the generator per partner

say.en: Partners have wishes: one wants the E S G template, another only some share classes, a third no documents. Handle these in configuration, not in code. The register says which blocks and templates each partner gets, and the generator follows it. A copy of the generator per partner is the fastest way into the trouble you saw in the first film of this series.

Generation usually has a short time window: between the approval of the data in the evening and the cut-off time of the partners. Generate funds in parallel, one fund per task. Start each delivery as soon as its data is approved, not at a fixed late hour. And measure how long it takes, so that you notice early when growth makes it too slow.

items.head: The difficult cases
items.text: A correction, a fund without positions, a second currency.

say.en: Test with golden files: a fixed set of input data and the file it must produce. After every change, the generator runs again, and the result is compared with the golden file, then validated and checked. Include the difficult cases: a correction, a fund without positions, a share class in a second currency.

en.title: Automated on every change
en.code:
end-to-end                                        success
  start PostgreSQL 16                             ok
  fetch the examples and the 4.2.9 schema         ok
  load the realistic files                        ok
  load them again: every file skipped             ok
  export the Multi-Asset fund                     ok
  validate the export (XSD 1.1)                   ok
  correction (AMEND): assets unchanged            ok
  reconciliation queries                          ok

say.en: Automate the tests. In the reference implementation, every change runs through the same steps on GitHub: start the database, load the example files, export them again, validate the export, run the data-quality checks. A change that breaks the output is noticed before it reaches a partner.

After the checks, the file is handed over. It gets the agreed name, is compressed if it is large, and goes out on the agreed channel. Where possible, the receiver confirms that it arrived. And the file goes into the archive, together with its validation result, so that it can always be found again by its document ID.

items.head: Never regenerate it silently
items.text: The data may have changed since.

items.head: Changed content
items.text: Is a correction, with a new ID.

say.en: Sometimes a partner asks for a file again. Send the archived file, unchanged and with the same document ID. Do not generate it again from the database, because the data may have changed since, and the partner would receive different numbers under the same ID. If the content has to change, that is a correction, with a new ID.

items.head: Mapping table next to the code
An example file for every kind of delivery

say.en: Finally, document the generator. Keep the mapping table next to the code and change both together. Keep a short change log for your partners: what changed in the deliveries, and from when. And keep one example file for every kind of delivery. When a partner asks how a field is filled, the answer is found in minutes.

That was generating FundsXML: the target first, a clear mapping, careful formats, several versions, and automatic tests. In the last film of this series, you see how to run all this in daily operations. Thanks for watching.
